title: What the stock market actually is
concept: The stock market is a place where people buy and sell small ownership stakes in companies. When you buy a share of Apple, you own a tiny piece of Apple — and if Apple grows, your piece grows with it. Most people think the market is like a casino. It's not. Casinos have negative expected value. The stock market, over long periods, has always gone up.
takeaway: Owning stocks means owning real businesses. Long-term, that has always paid off.

scenario.situation: Your friend says the stock market is just gambling and refuses to invest. You have $1,000 to put somewhere for the next 10 years.

choices.text: Put it in a savings account — at least it's safe
Invest it in a broad index fund and leave it alone
Wait until the market 'calms down' before investing

feedback.A: Safe, but your savings account probably pays 0.5% interest. Inflation runs at ~3%. You're losing purchasing power every year.
feedback.B: Correct. A broad index fund over 10 years has historically returned ~10%/year. Your $1,000 becomes roughly $2,590.
feedback.C: The market never 'calms down' — it's always volatile. Waiting is just missing gains. Time in the market beats timing the market.

scenario.lesson: Time in the market beats timing the market. Every year you wait costs you compounding.

title: Risk is not a dirty word
concept: Risk means the chance your investment bounces around in value. Higher risk often comes with higher long-term returns. Zero risk usually means your money barely keeps up with inflation. The goal isn't to avoid risk — it's to take the right amount for your timeline.
takeaway: Match risk to when you need the money. Long horizon → you can ride out volatility.

scenario.situation: You're 27 and saving for retirement in 35 years. A co-worker says you should keep everything in cash 'to be safe.'

choices.text: Use a diversified stock-heavy portfolio because you have decades
Put it all in one hot stock your cousin mentioned

feedback.A: Cash feels safe, but inflation quietly erodes it. For 35 years, that 'safety' is expensive.
feedback.B: Correct. With a long timeline, volatility is your friend — you have time to recover and capture growth.
feedback.C: One stock is concentration risk, not a plan. Diversification is how ordinary people invest like institutions.

scenario.lesson: Timeline drives how much stock market volatility you can reasonably accept.

title: Index funds in plain English
concept: An index fund buys hundreds or thousands of stocks in one package, tracking an index like the S&P 500. You own a slice of the whole economy instead of betting on one company. Fees stay low because nobody is picking stocks by hand all day.
takeaway: Broad index funds are the simple default most people should start with.

scenario.situation: You're choosing your first retirement account investment. One option is an S&P 500 index fund with a 0.03% fee. Another is an actively managed fund with a 1.2% fee.

choices.text: Pick the active fund — higher fee must mean smarter people
Pick the index fund — keep costs tiny and own the whole market
Skip both and day-trade on your phone

feedback.A: Fees compound against you. A 1% drag over decades can cost six figures in lost growth.
feedback.B: Correct. Low-cost indexing is how you keep more of what the market returns.
feedback.C: Day trading is a hobby with bad odds, not a retirement strategy.

scenario.lesson: Fees are guaranteed; outperformance is not. Start cheap and diversified.

title: Dollar-cost averaging without the jargon
concept: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount on a schedule. Sometimes you buy high, sometimes low — it averages out and removes the urge to guess the perfect day to invest.
takeaway: Consistency beats guessing. Automation is your friend.

scenario.situation: You can invest $300 per month. The market just dropped 8% in a week.

choices.text: Pause contributions until things look better
Withdraw what you already invested to stop the bleeding

feedback.A: Pausing often means buying later at higher prices. You're timing the market emotionally.
feedback.B: Correct. Your fixed amount buys more shares when prices are lower — that's DCA working.
feedback.C: Selling after a drop locks in losses. Long-term investors add, they don't panic out.

scenario.lesson: Regular investing turns volatility into more shares at better average prices.

title: Why diversification actually matters
concept: Diversification spreads money across many companies, sectors, and sometimes countries. When one part of the economy struggles, another may do fine. It's the free lunch of investing — less drama for similar long-term returns.
takeaway: Don't bet your future on one story stock.

scenario.situation: Your entire portfolio is shares of the company you work for because you 'believe in the mission.'

choices.text: That's fine — you know the company best
Sell some and diversify — your job is already tied to that company
Borrow to buy more because conviction matters

feedback.A: Knowing the cafeteria menu isn't the same as predicting the stock. Concentration risk is real.
feedback.B: Correct. Your income and equity are already linked — diversify the rest.
feedback.C: Leverage plus concentration is how small setbacks become disasters.

scenario.lesson: Human capital + stock in the same firm = double exposure.
